units.title: Arbitrum Nitro and Orbit chains
angles: Known weaknesses. Collect security advisories, audit reports, bug bounty write-ups, incident post-mortems and open issues for this network's execution client, precompiles and system contracts from the last two years, including behaviour the network calls by design. For each, decide whether an ordinary account could use it against funds in the PoolManager.

Exits. Can an ordinary account make another user's swap or liquidity removal impossible to include or always revert on this network (gas caps, storage pricing, per-transaction limits, tick crossing cost, special recipients)?

units.title: OP Stack chains with a non-ETH gas token
angles: Pooled assets. Read the PoolManager's largest token balances on this network from chain. For each token, check transfer and balanceOf for behaviour any holder can trigger: rebasing, fees, callbacks, share accounting, special recipients, special amounts.

Faces. Find every way one balance at the PoolManager can be reached under two currency ids or in two units on this network (native asset with an ERC-20 face, wrapped native predeploys, bridged and canonical versions sharing storage, tokens with more than one entry point), and walk sync, settle, take, mint and burn across the two faces in every order.

code.task: The repository's own tests, NatSpec comments and test doubles are the only permitted reference for what the source is meant to do. Replay by reading or by Python transcription every concrete expectation in test/PoolManager.t.sol, test/PoolManager.swap.t.sol, test/PoolManager.clear.t.sol, test/PoolManagerInitialize.t.sol, test/ModifyLiquidity.t.sol, test/Sync.t.sol, test/CustomAccounting.t.sol, test/ERC6909Claims.t.sol, test/NoDelegateCall.t.sol, test/DynamicFees.t.sol, test/DynamicReturnFees.t.sol, test/SkipCallsTestHook.t.sol, test/Extsload.t.sol, test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.t.sol and test/types/Currency.t.sol against the source in src/, including every expectRevert selector and every asserted number. Compare each NatSpec comment in src/interfaces/ with what the implementation does. Read the helper contracts in src/test/ and test/utils/ for behaviour the production code is expected to have. Every place where the source cannot produce what a test or comment states is a candidate: decide whether it gives an ordinary account a way to take or lock funds.

The repository's own tests are the only permitted reference for what the libraries are meant to compute. Replay by Python transcription every concrete vector and boundary in test/libraries/ (TickMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, FullMath, BitMath, UnsafeMath, TickBitmap, Position, SafeCast, LiquidityMath, LPFeeLibrary, ProtocolFeeLibrary, Hooks, Lock, StateLibrary, Pool, and the rest), test/Tick.t.sol and test/types/, against the source in src/libraries/ and src/types/. Use the gas snapshot files in snapshots/ as a second witness: a snapshot that the source could not plausibly produce marks a changed code path. Every vector, revert or boundary the source cannot reproduce is a candidate: decide whether it gives an ordinary account a way to take or lock funds.

Answers leads L-153 and L-202; report both in leadResults. sync needs no lock and the unlock flag, the deltas and the synced currency all live in transient storage. For each of the 21 networks, name every feature that runs caller-chosen code against live state under a transient storage map other than the one of the surrounding transaction, or that discards or restores transient storage part way through a transaction while keeping persistent writes and token transfers. Candidates named so far: Tempo zone contracts, Tempo type 0x76 batches and the T14 ConfigurableAccount, Base transactions of type 0x79, Stylus host calls and retryable redeems on the Arbitrum family, coreReceiveWithData and sendToEvmWithData system calls on HyperEVM, PBH bundles on World Chain, the fee currency debit and credit calls on Celo, Arc CallFrom, MegaETH keyless deploy, Monad parallel execution and its JIT, simulation or sandbox precompiles anywhere, and EIP-7702 or account abstraction frames. For each, establish from node client source: can an ordinary contract start it from inside a call; does the inner run begin with an empty map, a copy, or the same map; are its persistent writes and token transfers kept when it returns; is transient storage journaled and rolled back on revert the same way as on Ethereum. Then walk unlock, sync, settle, settleFor, take, mint and burn through any feature that differs, and decide whether one payment can be credited twice, whether the lock can be seen as open or closed wrongly, or whether a delta can be dropped.

Answers lead L-203; report it in leadResults. settle credits msg.value as paid without looking at any balance (src/PoolManager.sol:352-354), and native take sends value with a plain CALL (src/types/Currency.sol:44-52). For each of the 21 networks, establish from node client source and on-chain tests whether a call frame can carry a nonzero CALLVALUE while the caller's balance does not fall by the same amount, or whether a value CALL from the PoolManager can succeed without the PoolManager's balance falling, or fall by a different amount than the value. Check: system caller rules (go-ethereum and BNB Smart Chain skip the balance check for caller 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe; can anything an ordinary account sends execute with that caller); deposit transactions with a mint field on OP Stack chains including the custom gas token chains; retryable tickets and unsigned L1 messages on the Arbitrum family; Tempo, where there is no native asset; Arc, where native value is USDC with blocklist checks and an 18 versus 6 decimal split; Celo token duality and the transfer precompile; Polygon's 0x1010 and state sync; HyperEVM system transactions and the 0x2222 bridge address; Monad reserve balance rules; MegaETH; Avalanche atomic transactions and its native asset precompiles; DELEGATECALL and CALLCODE value semantics on each client; SELFDESTRUCT to self and to the PoolManager; EIP-7702 delegated senders; value sent in sponsored, batched or fee-token transactions. For every difference, decide whether an ordinary account can obtain a native credit at the PoolManager it did not pay for, or drain native balance it is not debited for.

Answers lead L-166 and the zero amount take lead from cycle 2; report L-166 in leadResults. take lets anyone make the PoolManager call X.transfer(to, amount) on any address X, with amount zero at no cost, and send native value with empty calldata to any address. sync and settle credit any rise in X.balanceOf(PoolManager). For each of the 21 networks, look for an address X whose balanceOf(PoolManager) comes from a ledger that some call from the PoolManager raises (a value transfer, a zero amount transfer, a transfer to a special recipient), as EntryPoint.balanceOf and WETH9 do on Ethereum, and for which transfer(to, amount) from the PoolManager then pays out. For each such X work out the full cycle with numbers: what the caller is debited under which currency id, what it is credited, and whether the net leaves the caller with value that belonged to pools. Also list what sender-side logic a zero amount or dust transfer from the PoolManager triggers in the largest pooled tokens on each network (reward checkpoints, auto-claims, delegation changes, vesting releases, fee-on-transfer exemptions, rebase syncs), and whether an ordinary account can use the PoolManager as the sender to move or lock value that belongs to pools. Read the PoolManager's largest token balances from chain to pick the tokens.
